Cheats

Game guide

Economy, combat, movement, setup previews, and the live map. The terrain list at the end reflects the last map the game generated or loaded — use Generate New in solo setup, run a skirmish, or open the multiplayer lobby preview so those swatches match what you are playing on.

Borders and the setup preview

When you generate a procedural map, each faction’s capital seeds a distance-based territory; the game then balances land area between factions (± one tile when the map does not divide evenly) so borders stay smooth instead of jagged. Town count scales with buildable land so small maps are not carpeted in settlements. New towns are prioritized inside each faction’s compass wedge (same rotation as the first political pass) so they sit naturally in that side of the island instead of skewing into a neighbour’s heartland. Setup and lobby previews draw exact political ownership from the same hex data the match uses (cardinal neighbor edges, same faction colors).

In solo play, click Generate New when you want to lock in a layout: your last preview shares the same random seed as the very next Start provided you do not change map size, shape, or AI count before launching. If you skip preview entirely, each start still generates a full procedural map — it just will not match an older thumbnail sitting in the UI. Multiplayer reuses the lobby seed for both the lobby minimap and the host launch so every seat sees the same geography.

Core loop and victory

Your top-bar Income number is total $ per second after all controlled sources are counted. It includes $12/s command funding while you control a town, city income, and the separate Land stat shown beside it, so the Land value is a breakdown, not extra money outside the total.

Territory capture has a fixed footprint for each unit type: infantry and marines claim one tile ring, armor two, and ships one on water. The footprint is the same for players and AI and does not expand on empty ground. Enemy-occupied tiles and defended neighboring cells still block claims.

Every owned non-water territory tile contributes a small amount of $. Capturing more ground therefore matters even before you take another town, while the map’s starting split is balanced so players begin with matching territory income.

Domination ends the match once you have captured every enemy city — straggler armies no longer matter if they have nowhere left to drill or recruit. Annihilation ignores the scoreboard of towns: you must destroy every hostile combat unit, while unarmed trade convoys never count toward that tally.

Capturing a town

Every settlement owns a connected cluster of urban tiles (streets and built-up hexes tied to that city). The flag does not flip until you control the full cluster: every one of those urban tiles must be in friendly hands, with no defending combat presence on them, before ownership and income swap. Leaving a single urban tile contested or enemy-held keeps the town defender-owned, so surround and clear the built-up area methodically.

Once captured, garrison if you can — production can pause briefly while the town is still flagged as under combat pressure on that tick.

Fog of war & scouting

When fog is enabled, friendly territory reveals two tiles beyond its edge. Every unit scouts from its actual position: infantry and marines see five tiles, armor four, warships six, transports five and convoys three. Towns see five tiles and forts four; allies share sight. Moving units expand visibility even away from the frontline. Explored ground remains known after troops leave, but unseen enemy units and structures stay hidden.

AI factions use the same sight rules. Scouts explore unknown ground and sea routes; the AI can investigate the last known location of a discovered town, but cannot track hidden troops or observe hidden construction. Battle report → Players shows public land totals and spotted enemy forces. Enemy reserves, money, production and losses remain unknown until the battle ends.

Battle report

Open Stats for land tiles and land share, economy and spending, unit composition, production, readiness, supply, damage and losses. Reports use the same four tabs on desktop and phones. Mobilization totals exclude opening armies and menu battles; finished reports include every faction.

Structures and income

A factory is a major investment: it lifts both $ and manpower income and is required to train armor. A farm boosts manpower growth. A harbor raises $ a bit, and it is needed where the urban footprint touches open water so you can build ships from that port.

Cities provide the larger economy: each town adds base $ and manpower growth, factories increase both, farms raise manpower further, and harbors add extra $. Manpower growth is separate from $ income and is spent on training infantry, marines, ships, and armor.

Trade convoys spawn between linked cities and pay a one-time bonus when they dock. If your budget stays underwater, unpaid upkeep will start chewing down army health until you recover — watch the treasury before you max out every regiment.

Terrain, movement & combat tilt

Mountains block normal land movement. Infantry and armor use land routes in all eight directions without cutting corners through peaks, and cross completed bridges as land. Units avoid water unless directly ordered there, no land route exists, or a crossing saves a very large detour. The AI favors dry detours and useful bridges near its army. All units in water except ships and marines are out of supply: after ten full uninterrupted seconds out of supply, they lose 3.5% max HP per second, cannot heal, and move slowly, even under orders or beside a friendly town. Forts do not reduce water attrition. Marines move amphibiously without water attrition, but remain vulnerable to enemy fire afloat and display the blue embarkment icon; warships, transports and supply ships fight from water and are the only units that can heal there. Warships have 300 HP, matching armor toughness. Land and naval units damage one another within weapon range. Transports safely carry one land unit; they have only 50 HP. Marines cannot heal while afloat. These rules apply equally to players and AI. Supply ships keep nearby troops supplied within a fort-sized radius, including landed infantry and armor; they never protect ordinary troops swimming without a transport. Oceans, rivers and lakes are neutral water: they never count as territory or land income.

Attack % scales outgoing strikes vs the same regiment on baseline grass; Dmg taken % scales how hostile hits resolve on you (below 100% absorbs better; above 100% means more exposed).

Ocean headers: Ocean M/S = marines & ships on ocean (amphib for marines); Ocean drown ΔI / ΔA = infantry vs armor caught drowning in ocean—same wording as unit cards (Atk + Dmg taken rows).

Trade convoys are civilians—no terrain combat multipliers.

Values mirror getTerrainAttackModifier / getTerrainDefenseModifier. Fort (Dmg taken 80%), morale, unpaid upkeep (−2.5% max HP/s), and out-of-supply attrition are separate effects. Water uses the supply attrition rate once; it does not add a second drowning charge.

Combat and morale

Units open fire on their own when an enemy is inside their range. They can keep marching on their orders while they shoot, but only at about a third of normal speed.

Stress can break morale and send a formation routing. To recover, rest on safe owned ground with no enemies in suppression range so healing and cohesion ticks can fire (see healing below).

Construction and reinforcements

All towns start empty. Generated towns have at least one non-urban cell between their footprints. Buildings, forts and bridges take 60 seconds; mobilization takes 15 seconds for infantry, 20 for marines, 25 for heavy units, and 30 for ships, including campaign reinforcements. A small circle beside the city counts down to completion, then the arriving unit plays its deployment animation. Each town handles one order at a time. Pausing stops progress. Player and AI towns cannot recruit or complete production while under attack: combat, hostile troops on any town cell, or hostile control of part of the town pauses the queue until the threat clears. Paid progress is preserved. In campaigns, unit buttons call existing reserve reinforcements without charging money or manpower again. Undeployed reserves stay safe between battles.

Supply and the 10-second attrition timer

10-second grace period: a unit must remain out of supply for ten full seconds of game time before supply attrition damages it. A yellow countdown appears above the unit; its effects page shows the remaining time. Restoring supply or boarding a transport resets the clock. Pausing stops the timer; 2× and 3× advance game time faster. Healing is blocked while out of supply, including during the countdown. This rule is identical for your troops and the AI. Ships and marines are exempt from water attrition; ordinary troops swimming without a transport are not protected by supply ships.

Starting armies deploy on friendly land connected to an owned town. About 20% cover the supplied border evenly and 80% start near towns, with armor in the rear. Empty offshore holdings count toward balanced land ownership but receive no starting land troops.

Every friendly town supplies its connected friendly land, including a captured enemy town. A surrounded pocket containing a friendly town remains supplied: its units take no encirclement damage and can recover when safe. Units lose land supply only when they have no cardinal land connection to any friendly town. These supply, warning and attrition rules apply equally to player and enemy armies, including when hostile territory is captured underneath a unit. Such pockets are marked encircled. Units receive ten uninterrupted simulation seconds out of supply before taking 3.5% max HP attrition per second; they cannot heal during this grace period. Regaining city or supply-ship supply, or boarding a transport, resets the countdown. Moving between unsupplied land and water does not reset it. The warning above each unit and its effects page show the time remaining. Map edges and neutral borders do not supply a townless pocket. Marines only: a pocket connected to an ocean or river remains supplied for marines, as though it had a town connection. Infantry and armor in the same coastal pocket still need a friendly town. Forts only halve unsupplied attrition. Active fighting at a town can pause production even while it supplies its territory.

Island landings: landing on an island without a town captures only the normal area around your units. Its remaining coastal territory does not surrender automatically or count as an encircled land pocket. Fully surrounded inland remnants can still transfer. Infantry and armor on a townless island still need a friendly town connection for supply; marines retain their water-supply exception.

Healing

Regeneration ticks only when the hex is yours, the unit is supplied (a land route to a town, or marine-only ocean/river supply), and there are no hostile combat units threatening the area. HP, manpower, and morale all inch back together, shown with the small green + pulse only while strength is actually being restored; the icon clears at full HP and manpower.

Unit status effects

While a condition is active, units show an icon above the marker when applicable, plus matching detail pills on the unit sheet. Each card below uses your equipped unit skin (trade convoys always use gold markers).

Orders on desktop

Click or box-select troops; Shift-click a friendly unit to add it to the selection. Save selected troops with Ctrl + 0–9; press the number or click its HUD group to recall them. Issue moves with a right-click. With troops selected, Shift + left-click or right-click on the map appends waypoints and keeps the group’s formation. Shift-drag a line to queue a new formation, or drag from a selected unit to paint a movement stroke.

Touch controls

The unit card has Move, Waypoint, and Formation buttons. Pick a mode, then click or tap the map. Waypoint mode keeps appending destinations; dragging places a formation-line waypoint. Board and Unload appear in the same order bar when transports are available. Camera zoom and pan retain their usual gestures.

Unit types

Each class below uses the classic marker style (always shown here, regardless of your equipped skin). Combat units follow your skin in play; trade convoys always use the gold square or gold ship wedge shown below.

Infantry

Your bread-and-butter land fighters: cheap to raise, flexible on most terrain, and ideal for skirmishing, capping urban tiles, and screening heavier columns. They pay normal combat penalties when attacking into rough ground or cities but are not as debuffed as heavies.

Armor (factory)

Armored formations unlocked once the city builds a factory. They cost far more $ but only use 1k manpower, hit harder, and absorb more; they are deliberately clumsy assaulting woods, hills, swamps, towns, mountains, or water — use them as breakthrough wedges on open ground instead of forcing frontal pushes into dense terrain.

Marines

Amphibious specialists. They fight at full attack strength and move at 62% speed on water tiles and cope well on coastal sand, but take a damage penalty on drier inland terrain. Use them for beach landings and fighting on the water grid where regular infantry are heavily slowed.

Transports (harbor)

A fragile ship that carries exactly one land unit safely across water. Costs $2,000 and 1,000 MP; 18-second mobilization. 50 HP, 500 crew and half infantry firepower. Transports count as boats for supply, attrition and repair rules. Select a land unit and right-click an empty friendly transport, or use Board transport. Both meet at a reachable shore. Select the loaded transport and right-click land, or use Unload for the nearest clear shore. An occupied landing waits until clear. Passengers cannot fight, heal or suffer attrition aboard; if the transport sinks, its passenger is lost. Era-appropriate barges, galleys, sailing transports and landing craft share these rules.

Supply ships (harbor)

Mobile naval logistics for beachheads. Costs $2,400 and 1,000 MP; 22-second mobilization. 50 HP, 500 crew and half infantry firepower, matching a transport’s weakness. Nearby friendly troops count as supplied within the same radius as a fort, including marines and landed infantry or armor. Passengers remain protected aboard transports. Ordinary land units swimming without a transport still suffer water attrition after ten seconds. Supply does not let marines or infantry heal afloat. Select a supply ship to see its range. Protect it with warships; losing it can isolate the landing force. Each era and unit pack has a matching supply vessel with a cargo-crate mark.

Warships

Built from harbors, these hulls live entirely on the water mesh. They duel other fleets, screen amphibious wedges, and can interdict lanes, but they will never march inland or flip a town by themselves — team them with infantry that can actually enter the urban tiles.

Trade convoy (overland)

Unarmed haulers spawned between partnered cities. They ignore combat orders, do not contribute to annihilation scoring, and exist purely to deliver lump income when they finish the route. Routers try to skirt hot corridors when a safer detour exists.

Trade convoy (sea lane)

The same economic unit when the pathfinder chooses an ocean hop: still defenseless, still paid only on docking, still invisible to the “kill every army” win condition — just faster when bluewater movement beats hugging every beach tile.

Formations and multi-select

Giving one move order to many selected regiments distributes their destinations along a shallow line aimed perpendicular to the overall advance. That keeps a broad stack from piling onto a single hex and clogging choke points the moment the order lands.

Nothing stops you from detaching a subgroup with another click or issuing a shorter stroke if you deliberately want a tighter clump for urban brawls; formations are a convenience default, not a hard constraint.

Convoy economics

Convoys bridge production pockets: they spawn on timers from connected cities, attempt to avoid obvious kill boxes, and pay their lump sum the moment they unload. Shut them down economically by taking the endpoints or hunting them mid-route — just remember they never satisfy annihilation by themselves.
